cf.title: Mark the enum comparison functions as leakproof

verdict_reasoning: The reported need is enum equality only (messages #4 and #5), and message #3 already accepts enum_eq as safe. demand-1 and demand-2 show that enum_cmp and the ordering operators have no user case and no measurement, while message #3 sets a performance bar for them. The list has to agree on the scope before code review makes sense. Only 3 of 5 messages were visible in full, so confidence is medium.

brief.title: Mark the enum comparison functions as leakproof
brief.problem: Under row-level security, predicates on enum columns cannot be used as index conditions because enum_eq and enum_cmp are not leakproof. Users with enums in indexes and composite primary keys see severe performance regressions once they enable RLS.
brief.proposed_design: The patch sets the leakproof flag on the enum comparison functions in pg_proc.dat and updates the opr_sanity regression output. The author argues that the only side channel is error messages, and that none of the reachable errors reveal the compared values. He also proposes that a leakproof proof only needs to consider attacks through an application, not arbitrary SQL, and may ignore out-of-memory errors.
user_visible_surface: enum_eq, enum_cmp and the other enum comparison functions show proleakproof = true in pg_proc
Planner can push enum comparisons into security barrier views and RLS quals, including as index conditions
author_claims: Errors reachable from enum_cmp_internal() occur only for non-enum input or data corruption, which SQL cannot trigger.
Cache memory allocations reveal only pg_enum contents, which are already public.
Out-of-memory errors that show allocation sizes cannot be exploited through an application.
Text comparison is already leakproof and has a larger detoast OOM risk than enum_cmp.
A customer depends on enum comparisons working with RLS.
brief.thread_state: Tom Lane wants to reject enum_cmp because its code is too large to confirm safe now and after future changes, but he agrees enum_eq is safe. Laurenz says only equality matters to the user but cites an earlier argument that enum_cmp can stand in for enum_eq; nobody has answered that point.
unclear: Whether a patch marking only enum_eq leakproof would be acceptable, given the earlier argument that enum_cmp can stand in for it.
Which of the enum comparison functions the patch marks; the material shows only the file list.
The thread has no benchmark of the RLS performance cost with enum predicates.
Nobody has answered whether the proposed narrower threat model for leakproof is acceptable.
Nobody has replied about the array operators Andreas Lind lists, and they are outside the patch.

prior_attempts.title: Row Level Security, leakproof-ness, and performance implications
prior_attempts.quote: I think that approach has been found not to actually satisfy the leakproofness criteria.
prior_attempts.reason: Peter Eisentraut wrote that redacting error messages had been found not to satisfy the leakproofness criteria, and Joe Conway accepted that the consensus was against him. Robert Haas suggested doing it outside core, with a logging hook and functions marked leakproof by hand, and doubted that customers could be supported with redacted messages. Peter also found the CREATE POLICY page the wrong place for the documentation patch and asked how a list of non-leakproof operators would be kept complete. The visible messages do not show which of these two patches this entry is.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P1's patch marked enum_eq and enum_ne, and its thread also discussed redacting error messages and a GUC to treat all functions as leakproof. This proposal adds enum_cmp, uses no redaction, and argues that the reachable errors reveal no compared values.

objections.title: Demand covers enum equality only, not enum_cmp or ordering operators
objections.failure_scenario: The patch marks enum_cmp and the ordering operators leakproof even though no user in the thread needs them. Later changes to the enum cache or catalog lookup code then carry a leakproof obligation that a reviewer can miss. If such a change adds an error that leaks, RLS deployments with enums are exposed for a benefit nobody asked for.
objections.argument: The only concrete user names enum_eq as the function that blocked index conditions (message #5), and the author confirms that "only equality comparisons are important" (message #4). Tom Lane objects to enum_cmp only and accepts enum_eq (message #3). The one argument for including enum_cmp is that it can stand in for enum_eq, and the thread does not answer it. As things stand, the riskier half of the patch has no demand behind it.
objections.author_must_show: Which real query needs a range or ordering enum predicate as an index condition under RLS, and why would marking only enum_eq not serve it?

critic.reasoning: Messages #4 and #5 confirm that the reported need is equality only. The one reason given for enum_cmp is the substitution argument in message #4, and the thread shows no concrete case for it.

objections.title: No measurement shows the cost clears the bar used for text_cmp
objections.failure_scenario: A committer weighs the risk of enum_cmp against its benefit and finds no number for the benefit. The only user in the thread reports that workarounds exist for every function on his list. The leakproof promise, which is hard to take back, then rests on the needs of one customer.
objections.argument: Tom Lane says text_cmp was an exception because the performance cost of not marking it was unacceptable (message #3). The thread gives no benchmark, plan, or slowdown figure for enum predicates under RLS. Andreas Lind writes that "we eventually found workarounds for all of these issues" (message #5). Demand has lasted since at least the earlier attempt on enum_eq [P1], which supports equality but does not measure the cost for ordering operators.
objections.author_must_show: What slowdown do users see with enum ordering predicates under RLS, measured on a real schema, and why is the workaround Andreas Lind used not acceptable?

precedents.title: Row Level Security, leakproof-ness, and performance implications

critic.reasoning: Message #3 sets a performance bar for enum_cmp, and the thread has no plan, benchmark or slowdown figure. Message #5 reports that workarounds exist, so the material does not show that the bar is met.

other_surviving.title: Narrowed leakproof threat model would apply to every future marking
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A deployment gives RLS-restricted roles direct SQL access, as REST-to-SQL gateways do. A later function gets marked leakproof under the rule that only attacks through an application count, and that role then reads hidden rows through error text or timing in a pushed-down qual.
other_surviving.argument: Message #1 asks the project to accept that leakproofness needs to cover only attacks through application parameters and may ignore OOM errors. The patch's own case does not need this, but its commit message rests on that reasoning, and the rule would set the bar for later markings. Message #1 points to EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) as a known gap, but a known gap does not justify a weaker rule. Nobody answered this in the thread, and [P1] records that an earlier attempt to relax the criteria was turned down.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Can the enum_eq and enum_cmp case be argued under the existing rule, which counts arbitrary SQL from the restricted role, so the threat model stays unchanged?

other_surviving.argument: Message #3 says enum_cmp reaches too much code to confirm it is safe now and after future changes. Message #4 answers that a new error is unlikely to print an argument, but nothing in the patch enforces that. Message #4 also says the user needs only equality. It cites an earlier claim that enum_cmp can stand in for enum_eq, and that claim was not tested in the thread.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Would a patch marking only enum_eq and enum_ne meet the reported need, and in what concrete case does enum_cmp stand in for enum_eq so that it must be leakproof too?

critic.reasoning: Message #3 states this concern, and message #4 answers only that a leaking error is unlikely. No existing leakproof marking has such a test either, but message #3 treats small code size as the guard, and enum_cmp does not have it.

refuted.title: The proposal narrows the leakproof threat model for all functions
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch marks another function leakproof by citing the rule from message #1: only attacks through an application count, and OOM errors can be ignored. A user with direct SQL access then learns hidden row values through an allocation-size error or through a cost-dependent error path. Nobody finds out until someone reports it as a security issue.
refuted.argument: Message #1 asks the list to accept a weaker standard for leakproof in general, and the OOM part of the case for enum_cmp depends on it. In [P1] a similar loosening was turned down: redacting error messages "has been found not to actually satisfy the leakproofness criteria", which shows the criteria count leaks to any SQL user. Message #3 restates the strict standard, and no reply in the thread accepts the narrower model.
refuted.author_must_show: Can the case for this patch stand under the existing threat model, where an attacker runs arbitrary SQL and OOM errors count?

refuted.title: Narrower leakproof threat model is proposed but the documented definition stays
refuted.failure_scenario: An extension author reads the LEAKPROOF rationale committed with this change and marks their own functions leakproof under the narrower rule, which ignores direct SQL and allocation-size errors. A user who can run arbitrary SQL under RLS then reads hidden values from error messages. The author finds out from a security report, and the documentation still promises the stricter guarantee.
refuted.argument: Message #1 asks the project to judge leakproofness only against attacks through an application, and to ignore OOM errors. The CREATE FUNCTION documentation defines LEAKPROOF without that limit, and the patch touches no documentation. Message #3 rejects enum_cmp under the existing standard, and nobody in the thread accepts the narrower model. If enum_cmp is accepted on the narrower model, the user-facing contract changes silently and no longer matches earlier leakproof decisions.
refuted.author_must_show: Does the case for enum_cmp hold under the LEAKPROOF definition now documented, or would the documentation need to change too?

refuted.title: Leakproof enum_cmp ties a large code path to an unchecked invariant
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch to catcache, the enum cache or load_enum_cache_data() adds an error that prints a datum or an OID derived from the compared value. No regression test fails, and the leak is found only in a security report after release.

Message #4 answers that new errors are unlikely to print the arguments, which is a forecast and puts no guard in place. The proof in message #1 runs through syscache lookups and cache building, code that other features change often. [P2] records that developers changing such code are unlikely to find a written rationale.

The site that wanted the speedup could instead have accepted that risk on its own.

committability.liability: For enum_cmp, the owner signs that no present or future error path in the enum cache, syscache lookup or pg_enum scan reveals a compared value. No test checks this, and it has no end date. For enum_eq alone the liability is small.

precedents_retrieved.title: enum support in btree_gin and btree_gist
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds enum support to the btree_gin and btree_gist extensions, without distance operators and so without KNN support. The enum comparison goes through enum_cmp_internal, which uses the type cache for enums whose values are not in OID order.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Testing showed that GiST comparisons gave wrong results after alter type ... add value, because enum_cmp_internal expects fcinfo->flinfo and DirectFunctionCallN passes NULL. Tom Lane judged a NULL check too slow and said the proper fix is to pass the FunctionCallInfo through the btree_gist/gin intermediate layer, which touches almost every function. The author agreed but had no time to do this before the end of the commitfest.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The problem is that the intermediate layer in btree_gist (and
probably btree_gin too, didn't look) does not pass through the
FunctionCallInfo data structure that's provided by the GIST AM.

precedents_retrieved.title: Document the limitations of row-level security
precedents_retrieved.summary: Pierre Ducroquet proposed a documentation patch, placed on the CREATE POLICY reference page, that lists performance-affecting restrictions of row-level security caused by built-in operator functions not being marked leakproof. The thread began with a patch that marks functions such as enum_eq/enum_ne and textin/textout leakproof and raised wider questions about leakproofness for array operators and functional indexes.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Peter Eisentraut agreed that the leakproofness of built-in operators should be documented better, but said the CREATE POLICY reference page was the wrong place for it. He also said that such a list would be expected to be complete and maintained, while the patch covered only a few cases the author had found. He judged that the patch needed significant additional work and set it to returned with feedback.

Also, once you start such a list, there will be an expectation that it's
complete.  So that would need to be ensured.

precedents_retrieved.title: revamp row-security tracking
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch replaces the per-query tracking of whether row security applies with a global queue of row-security nest levels. get_row_security_policies() marks the levels, and higher-level callers such as fireRIRrules() read them, with cleanup after an ERROR.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Dean Rasheed objected to the global variables, the hooks into transaction management, and setting the flag far from where RLS policies are applied. He proposed adding a hasRowSecurity output parameter to fireRIRrules() instead. The author wrote that design as v2 but worried it did not go far enough, and later planned to withdraw for lack of interest. Tom Lane replied that the topic needs more thought and suggested other designs, and the visible messages show no work after that.
matched_queries: row level security index condition leakproof
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I'm also not a fan of using global variables in this way, or the
resulting need to hook into the transaction management system to tidy
up. The end result is that the places where the flag is set are moved
further away from where RLS policies are applied, which IMO makes the
code much harder to follow.

roaster_notes.note: Message #1 points to three earlier threads and message #4 to one more, but the material does not include their content. P1's recorded reason concerns error redaction and does not block marking enum_eq leakproof, which message #3 accepts as safe. P4 concerns documentation placement and does not apply here.
The change touches no syntax, GUC or psql behaviour, and pg_dump does not emit built-in function properties. Plans change under RLS only by allowing pushdown, so query results stay the same.

The patch only flips proleakproof on built-in enum functions in pg_proc.dat and needs a catversion bump. pg_upgrade rebuilds pg_proc from the new initdb.
